A2.text:
Oliver is a young lawyer from London. He lives in Baku. His best friend Yunus is a clever potter in Icherisheher. Baku is a multicultural city, but Yunus loves old Azerbaijani traditions.

Tomorrow is the famous Novruz holiday. Yunus invites Oliver to his family’s house for a big dinner.

“We have a special custom for this holiday,” Yunus says. “Everybody jumps over a fire in the yard. It is a fun spring ritual.”

Oliver is nervous, but he wants to be a good guest. He goes to a shop and buys traditional folk sweets, called pakhlava, for the family.

In the evening, the family makes a bright fire in the garden. Yunus’s grandmother, Lala, sits on a comfortable chair and watches everyone.

“Go on, Oliver, jump!” Yunus says.

Oliver runs fast and jumps over the fire. He safely clears the flames, but he jumps too high. Suddenly, his right shoe falls off his foot. It flies through the air and lands exactly on Grandmother Lala’s lap!

Oliver stops. He is very embarrassed and his face is red.

But Grandmother Lala looks at the shoe and laughs loudly. She gives it back and hands Oliver a glass of hot tea.

“Your shoe is safe,” she says. “Welcome to our family!”

B1.text:
Oliver, a young British lawyer living in Baku, often visits his good friend Yunus, a talented potter in the old streets of Icherisheher. Oliver enjoys the city's modern, multicultural vibe, but he really wants to understand the rich local heritage.

When the famous Novruz holiday arrives, Yunus invites Oliver to a big family gathering in his courtyard. He explains a popular local superstition about the spring holiday.

“If you jump over a fire on the last Tuesday before the new year, you leave all your bad luck and sadness behind,” Yunus says. “It is a very old ritual that we pass down to our children.”

Oliver wants to be a respectful guest. “Well, when in Rome, do as the Romans do,” he smiles. To prepare, he goes to a local market and buys a large box of famous folk sweets as a traditional gift for the hosts.

That evening, Yunus's family builds a roaring bonfire in the courtyard. Yunus’s elderly grandmother, Lala, watches the celebration from the porch with a warm smile.

When it is Oliver's turn, he steps up to the fire. He takes a deep breath, runs, and jumps as high as he can. He clears the hot flames easily, but unfortunately, his loose left shoe flies off his foot! The shoe sails through the smoky air and lands right in Grandmother Lala’s lap.

Oliver freezes, and his face turns completely red. He expects her to be annoyed by the clumsy foreigner. However, Lala just examines the shoe and begins to laugh heartily. She hands the shoe back to him along with a glass of hot tea.

“Do not worry,” she says warmly. “We have a long custom of welcoming everyone, even flying shoes!”

B2.text:
After two years working as a corporate lawyer in Baku, Oliver thought his cultural assimilation was nearly complete. He could effortlessly navigate the multicultural streets of the capital and drink incredibly strong black tea without a single drop of milk. But his close friend Yunus, a master potter with a dusty workshop in Icherisheher, insisted that Oliver still had much to learn about true Azerbaijani heritage.

For the upcoming Novruz festival, Yunus invited him to his family's spacious courtyard in Yasamal. “We are going to light a massive bonfire,” Yunus explained, meticulously painting a clay bowl. “Our ancestors believed the sacred flames would burn away the winter's hardships and purify the soul. It is a powerful superstition that we proudly pass down through the generations.”

“I suppose old habits die hard,” Oliver laughed, admiring the intricate pottery on the shelves. “But when in Rome, do as the Romans do, right? I will gladly jump over the fire.”

Determined to respect the local custom, Oliver purchased a premium box of Sheki halva and memorized a couple of traditional folk greetings. When he arrived at the house, the courtyard was already glowing with bright firelight. Yunus's grandmother, Lala, sat wrapped in a thick woollen shawl on the porch. She cheerfully supervised the ritual as excited relatives took turns leaping over the crackling flames.

When his turn came, Oliver took a deep breath, ran, and launched himself into the air. He cleared the fire perfectly with an athletic bound. Unfortunately, he was wearing a loose leather loafer. Mid-flight, the shoe slipped off his heel, sailed gracefully through the smoky air, and landed directly into Grandmother Lala's lap.

The lively music abruptly stopped. Oliver froze in absolute horror, expecting the elderly matriarch to be furious at his clumsiness. Instead, Lala picked up the warm shoe, examined it carefully, and began to roar with laughter.

“Next year,” she chuckled, handing the embarrassed lawyer a glass of pear-shaped tea, “we must definitely tie your shoes with a strong knot. But your adventurous spirit is very welcome here.”

podcast.title: Jumping over the fire

before.predict: What is your favourite holiday tradition? Guess: who in this episode jumped over a fire — Leyla or Sam?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is culture and traditions. And I have to tell you about my first Novruz.
[laugh] Oh yes. I was there.
In March my friends in Baku invited me to celebrate. And in the evening, everyone started jumping over small fires!
That's one of our oldest customs. It's a ritual for a new start — you leave the problems of the old year behind.
I was nervous. But my friend said, "When in Rome…" So I jumped too.
And you were great! Only your trousers were in a little danger.
[chuckle] Then there were the sweets — shekerbura, pakhlava. I ate far too many.
That food is part of our heritage. My grandmother makes shekerbura the way her mother did, and her mother before that.
That's lovely. Who taught you?
She did. Every year we make them together. I think every family needs to pass something down — a recipe, a song, a story.
Do you have any superstitions?
[laugh] Some. My grandmother says you mustn't whistle in the house, or money will leave. I don't believe it, but I still never whistle at home.
Old habits die hard!
Exactly. What about your family, Sam?
In England, at Christmas, we pull crackers and wear silly paper crowns. Nobody knows why. It's just what we do.
I think the best cities are multicultural. In Baku you can eat food from twenty countries on one street.
London is the same. But it's important not to lose your own culture. Assimilation is one thing — forgetting where you're from is another.
I agree. My ancestors lived in the mountains, and we still sing their folk songs at weddings.
That's beautiful. I'd love to hear one.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what is one tradition from your family that you want to keep — and why?
Mine is the silly paper crown. See you next time!
Bye for now!
